turns.t: Good afternoon. Mr Harold Bellamy? Have I got the right gentleman?
Harold, yes. Well, Harry. Everyone says Harry. Bellamy, yes.
Harry it is. And you are?
I'm Gwen, his daughter. I'm here most days. I'll fill in what he can't.
Good. I'm told the problem is the bowels. Harry, tell me in your words.
Constipation. I haven't been, um, for days. Four days. No, five. Gwen?
Five days since it last properly went, Dad. I wrote it down this morning.
Right. And did it start suddenly, or has it been creeping up?
It was last week. Or the week before. I really couldn't say.
I couldn't give you a date either. He's always been a bit slow, but it got worse some time ago.
Fine, we'll leave the start date. Any bloating or tummy discomfort now?
I feel bloated. Like a drum. Like a football, really.
Any vomiting?
No, no vomiting. Just full.
Good. Gwen, which medicines is he taking? I want every one.
Amlodipine, 5 mg every morning.
Amlodipine 5 mg in the morning. Next?
Aspirin, 75 mg, once a day, with his breakfast.
The little pink one. Is it pink? Or is it white?
Dad, the pink one is the aspirin, I do it every breakfast. Leave the tablets to me.
We'll stay with the aspirin. And the third?
Co-codamol, for the arthritis in his hips. Two when it's bad, usually in the evening.
Co-codamol, as needed, for arthritis. Noted. Harry, what other health problems have you had?
A stroke. That's why I'm in the bed. It was... a few years ago. Four? Six?
Five years in March, Dad.
Five. Yes. And the blood pressure, the high blood pressure. And the arthritis.
Stroke, high blood pressure, arthritis. Anything I've missed?
That's all of it.
Right. And who lives here with him?
Mum died, so it's just Dad here. I stay over, three nights a week. A carer pops in as well.
Good. How are your waterworks, Harry? Passing water without trouble?
Fine. Fine, thank you. Normal.
Let me do your readings. Arm out, Harry.
Blood pressure 142 over 80. Pulse 78. Temperature 36.6. Oxygen 96 percent. Breathing 16.
Is that all right for him?
Perfectly acceptable. Now Harry, I'm going to feel your tummy. Tell me if anything hurts.
Go on. Oh, that's cold. Your hands.
Sorry about that.
Your tummy is swollen and firm on the left side.
That's where it feels full.
And there's no tenderness when I press. No wincing.
I'm a tough old boot.
He is not, he cried at the telly yesterday.
Gwen!
Right. So here's what I want to do. I'd like to arrange an abdominal X-ray, to see what's going on inside.
Does he need to go to the hospital for it?
Yes, a transport service takes him and brings him back. The surgery will book it and ring you.
All right. That's fine.
Meanwhile, plenty of fluids, Gwen. A drink every hour he's awake. Prunes, porridge, whatever he'll eat.
I don't like prunes.
Then pears, or the juice. Whatever he'll take.
Pear juice. I can manage that. I think.
I'll sort it, Dad.
And keep giving the medicines exactly as you do now. Don't change anything till I've seen the X-ray.
Understood. Should I be worried?
You did the right thing calling us. I'll see you both again in one week, and we'll go through the picture.
One week. I'll be here. I'm not going anywhere, ha.
Thank you, doctor. I'll make us all a cup of tea before you go.
Kind of you, but I've another visit waiting. Take care, Harry.

social_history.description: Lives alone with daughter staying over three nights a week and a visiting carer

physical_examination.finding: Your tummy is swollen and firm on the left side

clinical_actions.description: Plenty of fluids and fibre-rich foods

clinical_uncertainties.description: Neither patient nor daughter can say when the constipation began.
